questions.q: State the formula for mechanical energy of an object of mass m moving with speed v at a height h above a chosen reference level. What is its SI unit?
questions.a: Mechanical energy = ½mv² + mgh; SI unit is joule (J). A wrong answer like "mv² + mgh" or "½mv² + ½mgh" reveals the student has not memorized the correct coefficients from the kinetic and potential energy formulas. Forgetting the unit or stating "watt" shows confusion between energy and power.

questions.q: A 2 kg ball is thrown vertically upward with an initial speed of 10 m/s. At the maximum height, its kinetic energy becomes zero. Explain why the mechanical energy of the ball-Earth system is still the same as at the start, and identify the energy transformation that occurs.
questions.a: At maximum height, kinetic energy is fully converted to gravitational potential energy (mgh_max). Since only gravity (a conservative force) does work, the total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant. A wrong answer claiming "energy is lost" or "mechanical energy decreases" reveals the misconception that energy disappears rather than transforms, or confusion between mechanical energy and kinetic energy alone.

questions.q: A 0.5 kg stone is dropped from a height of 20 m. Calculate its mechanical energy (i) at the start, (ii) after falling 5 m, and (iii) just before hitting the ground. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance.
questions.a:
(i) At start: v=0, h=20 m → KE=0, PE=mgh=0.5×10×20=100 J → ME=100 J.
(ii) After falling 5 m: h=15 m. Using v²=u²+2gh_fall=0+2×10×5=100 → v=10 m/s. KE=½×0.5×100=25 J, PE=0.5×10×15=75 J → ME=100 J.
(iii) Just before ground: h=0, v²=0+2×10×20=400 → v=20 m/s. KE=½×0.5×400=100 J, PE=0 → ME=100 J.
A wrong answer with different ME values at each stage indicates the student either miscalculated velocity/height or believes mechanical energy changes during free fall.

questions.q: Two identical balls are released from the same height: Ball A is dropped from rest, Ball B is thrown horizontally with speed 10 m/s. Compare their mechanical energies at the moment of release and just before hitting the ground. Assume no air resistance.
questions.a: At release: Ball A has ME = mgh (KE=0). Ball B has ME = mgh + ½m(10)² = mgh + 50m. Ball B has greater mechanical energy initially because of its horizontal kinetic energy. Just before hitting ground: Both have converted all potential energy to kinetic energy. Ball A: KE = mgh. Ball B: KE = mgh + 50m. Ball B still has greater mechanical energy. A wrong answer saying "both have same mechanical energy" reveals the student thinks mechanical energy depends only on height, ignoring the initial kinetic energy contribution.

questions.q: A student solves a pendulum problem: "A 1 kg bob is released from height 0.8 m. At the lowest point, its speed is 4 m/s. The student claims mechanical energy is conserved because KE at bottom = ½×1×4² = 8 J and PE at top = 1×10×0.8 = 8 J." Evaluate this claim. Is the student correct? Justify.
questions.a: The student is correct numerically (both equal 8 J) but the reasoning is incomplete. Mechanical energy conservation requires that the sum KE+PE is constant at ALL points, not just that the initial PE equals final KE. The student should verify at an intermediate point (e.g., at height 0.4 m, speed should be √(2g×0.4) ≈ 2.83 m/s, giving KE≈4 J, PE=4 J, sum=8 J). A wrong evaluation accepting the claim without checking intermediate points shows the student equates "initial PE = final KE" with "conservation at every instant."

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a ball, a ramp, and a meter scale to demonstrate that mechanical energy is conserved when a ball rolls down a smooth incline. Specify what you would measure, how you would calculate kinetic and potential energy at three points, and what result would confirm conservation.
questions.a: Set up a smooth ramp of length 2 m inclined at 30° (height 1 m). Use a 0.1 kg ball. Measure time to roll from rest at top to three points: top (h=1 m), middle (h=0.5 m), bottom (h=0). Calculate speed from distance/time (assuming uniform acceleration) or use v²=2gh for predicted speeds. At each point: KE=½mv², PE=mgh. Conservation is confirmed if KE+PE ≈ 1 J (mgh_initial) at all three points within experimental error. A poor answer that only measures final speed or ignores the middle point shows the student doesn't understand that conservation must hold at every instant, not just initial and final.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Mechanical energy is the total energy possessed by an object due to its motion and position, defined as the sum of its kinetic energy (energy due to motion) and potential energy (energy due to position or ______).

Fill in the blank: Watch a child on a swing in a playground: at the ______ points the swing momentarily stops (zero kinetic energy) but is at maximum height (maximum potential energy), while at the lowest point it moves fastest (maximum kinetic energy) at minimum height (minimum potential energy).
What is Mechanical energy? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Mechanical energy is the total energy possessed by an object due to its motion and position, defined as the sum of its kinetic energy (energy due to motion) and potential energy (energy due to position or configuration).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can calculate the total mechanical energy of a system at any instant by correctly computing kinetic energy (½mv²) and gravitational potential energy (mgh) with consistent reference levels, and can explain why mechanical energy remains constant in a closed system with only conservative forces acting.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Watch a child on a swing in a playground: at the highest points the swing ______ stops (zero kinetic energy) but is at maximum height (maximum potential energy), while at the lowest point it moves fastest (maximum kinetic energy) at minimum height (minimum potential energy).
